The Black-hooded oriole (Oriolus xanthornus) begins its life cycle as a hatchling emerging from an incubated bird egg that has been developing for 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days] at an incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a value inferred from data on the congeneric Eurasian golden oriole. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling weighed approximately 5.4 grams [Ww0 = approximately 5.4 grams], a modest neonatal mass that reflects the limited nutritional reserves carried over from the yolk-dependent embryo stage. This initial wet weight of 5.4 grams [Ww0 = 5.4 grams] is typical for a passerine of this size and marks the beginning of an intense period of parental provisioning. The nestling bird is entirely dependent on its parents for food and thermoregulation during the first several days of life, undergoing rapid organogenesis and feather development within the woven cup nest suspended in the forest canopy. The nestlings grow quickly as they transition from the organogenesis stage to the pin-feathered chick stage, although the first 14.5 days of life remain the most vulnerable period for brood mortality. Field observers have noted that the intense brood-rearing effort by both parents is critical to ensuring that the chicks survive this early developmental window.

The brood-rearing period culminates in fledging, a key developmental milestone that, under the warm thermal conditions typical of the species' tropical range (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), occurs at approximately 14.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 14.5 days after hatching], based on comparative observations of the closely related Oriolus oriolus. This fledging age of 14.5 days after hatching [tx = 14.5 days after hatching] marks the moment when the chick achieves its first flight and leaves the nest, although it remains dependent on its parents for food for several additional weeks at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The post-fledging dispersal phase follows shortly thereafter, as the young bird begins to forage independently and explore the surrounding habitat. During this time, the fledgling's flight feathers continue to mature, improving its aerial maneuverability and ability to evade predators. The relatively short nestling period, ending at 14.5 days after hatching [tx = 14.5 days after hatching], is consistent with the life history strategy of many tropical passerines that face high nest predation pressure and thus accelerate early development to minimize time in the nest at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Once independent, the immature bird enters a juvenile stage characterized by duller plumage and more tentative foraging behaviors.

Sexual maturation in the Black-hooded oriole proceeds gradually, with puberty attained at 43.5 days after hatching [tp = 43.5 days after hatching] under the prevailing ambient conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This age at puberty of 43.5 days after hatching [tp = 43.5 days after hatching] signals the onset of gonadal development and the production of mature gametes, though this does not immediately translate into reproductive activity at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The young bird must still acquire a territory and secure a mate before engaging in its first breeding attempt. This relatively early puberty, achieved at 43.5 days after hatching [tp = 43.5 days after hatching], allows individuals to enter the breeding population within the same year they hatched, an adaptation to the seasonally resource-rich environments of tropical forests at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Following gonadal maturation, the bird enters the sub-adult stage, during which it adopts the brilliant black-and-yellow adult plumage and begins to participate in territorial displays. The progression from fledgling to a reproductively viable organism is therefore completed within several weeks, a pace that is accelerated compared to many temperate-zone orioles. This rapid life history schedule is likely facilitated by the abundant insect prey available in the tropical canopy throughout much of the year.

The age at first successful reproduction, marking the transition to a breeding adult, occurs at approximately 401.5 days after hatching [tR = approximately 401.5 days after hatching], a value recorded at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] and representing about 1.1 years of life. This age at first brood of 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching] indicates that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year, investing their first year of life in somatic growth and territory establishment at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Breeding females, once reproductively active, achieve an ultimate wet weight of about 75 grams [Wwi = about 75 grams], a body mass that represents the maximum adult size for this sex. This adult body mass of 75 grams [Wwi = 75 grams] is at the higher end of the reported range for the species, which typically spans 46 to 79 grams for females, and reflects the energetic reserves necessary to support egg production and incubation. Clutch size is consistently reported as 3 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 3 eggs per nest], and the species typically rears two broods annually [F_R_i = two broods annually] during the peak of the breeding season. This reproductive output, comprising 3 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 3 eggs per nest] over two broods annually [F_R_i = two broods annually], enables a relatively high annual fecundity despite the per-clutch limitation of small clutch sizes typical for tropical forest birds.

Maximum longevity in the Black-hooded oriole has been documented at 9.8 years [am = 9.8 years] under the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] typical of its native lowland forests. This lifespan of 9.8 years [am = 9.8 years] is comparatively moderate for a passerine of its body size and reflects the trade-off between investing in reproduction and maintaining somatic health into later age classes at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The basal metabolic rate of a reproductively active adult, measured as a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 112.02 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 112.02 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], provides insight into the high energetic costs of maintaining daily activity in a tropical environment. This metabolic rate of 112.02 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 112.02 milliliters of oxygen per hour] is consistent with the elevated metabolic demands of a canopy-dwelling frugivore-insectivore that must sustain active foraging throughout the day at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The species exhibits a relatively high metabolic intensity for a bird of its mass, likely driven by the need to compete for territories and secure sufficient food resources to rear multiple broods each year. The maximum lifespan of 9.8 years [am = 9.8 years] thus represents the upper boundary that a few individuals attain under favorable conditions, though most likely die much earlier due to predation, disease, or resource competition at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
